h1: The 5 Best Ergonomic Keyboard and Mouse Sets of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Ergonomic Keyboard & Mouse: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: the 5 best ergonomic keyboard and mouse options of 2026, separating true split layouts from combos that only claim comfort.
summary: The Logitech Wave Keys is the best ergonomic keyboard in this set: a wave-curved deck, a cushioned rocking palm rest and Bluetooth or USB receiver pairing for $50 to $100. The Logitech Ergo K860 is the true split pick, and the Perixx PERIBOARD-512B is the budget split. Two under $25 combos add a mouse with a mild curve.
intro: Most keyboard and mouse sets sold as ergonomic are not. A flat keyboard paired with a slightly contoured mouse and the word on the box does almost nothing for wrist angle, and several well-known combos do not even claim it. Shoppers pay for a matched set and a label when the parts that matter are the keyboard layout and the shape of the mouse, which the packaging rarely explains.

We reviewed five options and dropped three well-known standard Logitech combos because their own listings describe a flat layout and an unshaped mouse. The five that remain are ranked on layout, palm support, connectivity and price tier, using spec sheets. The list says plainly which picks are keyboards only and which include a mouse, since two of the five ship without one.

products.name: Logitech Wave Keys Wireless Ergonomic Keyboard - Graphite
products.verdict: The keyboard that is actually ergonomic, in a compact body.
products.description:
The Wave Keys uses a wave-curved key deck on a single-piece frame with a rocking cushioned palm rest. It pairs over Bluetooth or a USB receiver, has a compact footprint and comes in graphite. It sells in the $50 to $100 bracket. A gentle wave lets your hands sit at a more natural angle than a flat deck, and the rocking rest supports the wrists as you move across the board.

It ranks first because the curved deck and palm rest change wrist posture without a steep learning curve. The K860 below is a more serious ergonomic design, but it takes more adjustment and costs more. Against the PERIBOARD, it adds wireless and a softer rest.

It suits most office workers. The caveat is that it is a keyboard only, so you need a separate mouse, and its ergonomics are gentler than a true split. Skip it if you want a matched pair.
products.idealFor: Office workers wanting a real ergonomic upgrade without a steep learning curve.
products.skipIf: You want a matched keyboard and mouse in one box.

products.name: Logitech Ergo K860 Wireless Ergonomic Split Keyboard with Wrist Rest
products.verdict: The most ergonomically serious keyboard here, with a true split layout.
products.description:
The Ergo K860 has a true split key layout, a full-width memory foam palm rest, reverse tilt to keep wrists more neutral, and Bluetooth for up to three devices. A Logi Bolt USB receiver is included. It sells in the $100 to $200 tier. A split layout separates the halves so your forearms angle in a natural line, rather than bending inward at the wrist.

It ranks second because it is the most ergonomically advanced option, but the split layout needs some adjustment time and it costs the most. The Wave Keys is the easier switch. Against the PERIBOARD, it adds wireless, memory foam and reverse tilt for a much higher price.

It suits heavy typists with wrist discomfort. The caveat is that you will want a vertical mouse to complete the setup. Skip it if you want a quick, easy switch.
products.idealFor: Heavy typists who want the most ergonomic layout.
products.skipIf: You want a quick, easy switch.

products.name: Perixx PERIBOARD-512B Wired Ergonomic Keyboard
products.verdict: A genuine split layout for the lowest price among true ergonomic boards.
products.description:
The PERIBOARD-512B has a genuine split key layout, a molded plastic wrist rest, a wired USB connection, a Windows-specific shortcut key row and a natural typing angle. It sells in the $25 to $50 bracket. Wired means no batteries and no pairing, and a single cable removes any lag concern for fast typists.

It ranks third because it gives the true split of the K860 for far less, but it is wired and has a plain plastic wrist rest instead of memory foam. Hard plastic adds height without the cushion of foam. Against the Wave Keys, it offers a more extreme layout at a lower price.

It suits budget buyers on Windows. The caveat is that it is not wireless and is a keyboard only. Skip it if you want wireless or a Mac layout.
products.idealFor: Budget Windows users wanting a true split.
products.skipIf: You want wireless or Mac layout.

products.name: Wireless Keyboard and Mouse Combo, Full Size Silent Ergonomic Keyboard and Mouse
products.verdict: A real keyboard and mouse pair with a modest ergonomic curve and quiet keys.
products.description:
This combo has a mildly curved full-size key layout, a standard sculpted mouse (not vertical), a single 2.4G USB receiver for both devices and quiet key switches. A long battery life is claimed. It sells for under $25. One receiver for two devices frees a USB port, and quiet switches suit shared offices and late-night work.

It ranks fourth because it is the only genuinely matched set that offers any curve, but the benefit is modest next to the Wave Keys. It costs a fraction as much. A sculpted mouse sits more comfortably than a symmetric one, though it keeps the wrist flat on the desk.

It suits budget buyers who want a matched set. The caveat is that the ergonomic gain is small and the mouse is not vertical. Skip it if you have real wrist pain.
products.idealFor: Budget buyers wanting a matched, quiet set.

products.name: Wireless Keyboard and Mouse Combo, 2.4G Full Size Silent Keyboard (Avocado Green)
products.verdict: The same budget matched-set idea in a distinctive color.
products.description:
This combo has a mildly curved full-size key layout, a 3-level DPI adjustable mouse, a single 2.4G USB receiver and an Fn multimedia key row in an Avocado Green colorway. It sells for under $25. Adjustable DPI lets you change pointer speed with a click, which helps on large monitors where a slow pointer wastes wrist motion.

It ranks fifth because its curve is as mild as the other combo's and its listing does not highlight silent switches the way the pick above does. The adjustable DPI mouse is its extra. Against the Wave Keys, it keeps the matched mouse but offers far less support.

It suits buyers who want a color-matched desk on a tight budget. The caveat is that ergonomic benefit is modest. Skip it if you need serious ergonomic support.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want a color-matched budget set.

whatMatters.factor: Split versus wave versus mild curve
whatMatters.detail: A true split divides the keys into two halves to reduce wrist angle. A wave curves the key deck gently, and a mild curve barely changes the layout. Check the listing for the phrase split and look at the pictures, not just the word ergonomic. The Ergo K860 and PERIBOARD list split, while the budget combos list a mild curve.

A cushioned or memory foam rest supports your wrists during long typing. A hard plastic rest adds height with less comfort. Look for the material named on the listing and for a full-width rest. The Ergo K860 lists memory foam, the Wave Keys a rocking cushion and the PERIBOARD molded plastic. Soft rests suit long sessions best.

Matched sets are convenient, but the mouse usually has little ergonomic shaping. Ergonomic keyboards are often sold alone. Check whether a mouse is included before assuming it. The Wave Keys, K860 and PERIBOARD are keyboards only, and two budget combos include a standard mouse that is not vertical. A mouse is half the setup.

Wired keyboards never need charging and have no lag, while wireless gives a cleaner desk. Bluetooth adds multi-device pairing and a USB receiver takes a port. Choose based on whether you switch devices. The K860 pairs three devices, while the PERIBOARD is wired only and needs no batteries. Wired also avoids pairing trouble.

Split layouts can slow typing for days or weeks as your hands adjust. Gentle curves are easier. Plan on a short adjustment period and check the return window. The Wave Keys has the shortest learning curve, and the Ergo K860 and PERIBOARD ask for more patience. Typing speed usually recovers within a few weeks.

faq.q: Do these come with a mouse?
faq.a: Only the two budget combos include one. The Wave Keys, Ergo K860 and PERIBOARD are keyboards only. Pair them with a mouse separately, ideally a vertical or sculpted one, since a flat mouse undoes some of the keyboard's gain.

faq.q: What is the biggest ergonomic set mistake?
faq.a: Trusting the word ergonomic on a flat combo. The keyboard layout and mouse shape matter. We left out standard flat Logitech combos for this reason. A mouse that forces the wrist flat matters as much as the keys.

faq.q: Is the K860 worth it over the Wave Keys?
faq.a: If you have wrist pain or type all day, yes. For most people the Wave Keys gives enough benefit for less. The split on the K860 needs more adjustment, and the memory foam rest adds comfort for long sessions. Try the return window if typing feels slow.

faq.q: How do I adapt to a split keyboard?
faq.a: Expect a slower typing speed for the first week and practice with the hand positions. Raise the palm rest height gradually. Keep wrists straight, as on the K860 or PERIBOARD. Stop and reset the rest height if forearms ache.

faq.q: How do I maintain an ergonomic keyboard?
faq.a: Wipe the keys and palm rest regularly and replace batteries on wireless models, like the Wave Keys or K860. Dust under keys with compressed air. Check the receiver connection if lag appears on the Wave Keys or budget combos. A USB extender can fix weak signal.

faq.q: Will these work with a Mac?
faq.a: Check the listing for OS support. The PERIBOARD has a Windows-specific shortcut row. Bluetooth keyboards like the Wave Keys and K860 generally pair, but key labels may differ, and the Windows row on the PERIBOARD will not map cleanly. Remap keys in the OS settings.

finalTake: Buy the Logitech Wave Keys for a real ergonomic upgrade without a steep learning curve. Move to the Ergo K860 if you type all day or have wrist discomfort, and the PERIBOARD-512B for a cheap true split on Windows. The two budget combos give a matched set with only a mild curve. Pair any keyboard-only pick with a mouse you like.
